reference.source: Postgraduate Haematology / Oxford Textbook of Medicine
clinicalPearls: The commonest inherited enzyme defect of the glycolytic pathway to cause chronic haemolytic anaemia, inherited in an autosomal recessive manner through PKLR mutations
It produces a lifelong non-spherocytic haemolytic anaemia of very variable severity, from mild to transfusion-dependent
Because the block is in glycolysis, upstream 2,3-diphosphoglycerate accumulates and shifts the oxygen dissociation curve, so anaemia is often better tolerated than the haemoglobin level suggests
Presentation ranges from neonatal jaundice and anaemia to gallstones, splenomegaly and iron overload in later life
Diagnosis relies on demonstrating reduced red-cell pyruvate kinase enzyme activity and confirmatory PKLR genetic testing, after excluding commoner causes
The blood film is non-specific, and characteristic echinocytes may become prominent only after splenectomy
Management includes folate support, transfusion when required, cholelithiasis surveillance, iron-overload monitoring, and splenectomy or newer targeted therapy in selected severe cases
reference.pathophysiology: Pyruvate kinase catalyses the final adenosine-triphosphate-generating step of glycolysis, the mature red cell's sole source of energy since it lacks mitochondria. Autosomal recessive PKLR mutations reduce enzyme activity, depleting cellular ATP and impairing the ion pumps and membrane maintenance that keep the red cell flexible, so cells become rigid, dehydrated and are removed prematurely, chiefly in the spleen and liver. The upstream metabolic block raises 2,3-diphosphoglycerate, which lowers haemoglobin oxygen affinity and improves tissue oxygen delivery, partly offsetting the anaemia; chronic haemolysis in turn produces jaundice, gallstones and, over time, iron loading.
additionalDifferentials: Hereditary spherocytosis and other membrane disorders
Other glycolytic or red-cell enzyme deficiencies
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count, reticulocyte count and blood film
Haemolysis markers including bilirubin, lactate dehydrogenase and haptoglobin
Direct antiglobulin test to exclude immune haemolysis
Red-cell pyruvate kinase enzyme activity assay (interpreted allowing for reticulocytosis)
PKLR gene sequencing for confirmation and counselling
Iron studies and ferritin to monitor for iron overload
redFlags: Aplastic crisis from parvovirus B19 with a sharp fall in haemoglobin
Iron overload with cardiac, hepatic or endocrine dysfunction
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is highly variable; many patients live well with intermittent support, while severely affected individuals face transfusion dependence, iron overload and gallstone complications, with splenectomy or targeted therapy able to reduce transfusion needs in selected cases.
pitfalls: Interpreting a normal-looking enzyme level without correcting for reticulocytosis, which can mask deficiency
Overlooking iron overload in patients who are not regularly transfused
Assuming the haemoglobin concentration reflects symptom burden despite the compensatory oxygen-delivery shift
Missing gallstones as a cause of recurrent biliary symptoms
